strengths: The paper tackles an important problem and proposes an ambitious synthetic-data pipeline, including a founder-level rather than trajectory-level holdout split.

Panda combines temporal and channel attention in a way that naturally supports varying numbers of variables. It shows promising improvements over the evaluated time-series foundation models across several metrics and forecast horizons on 9,300 generated test systems.

The evaluation is unusually broad in scope, covering simulated ODEs, three experimental datasets, two PDE examples, architectural ablations, masked completion, and a controlled study of training-system diversity.
Holding the number of training timepoints fixed while varying the number of systems is a useful experiment and provides credible evidence that dynamical diversity improves transfer.
weaknesses: The claimed breadth of out-of-domain generalization is overstated. The 9,300 test systems derive from only 20 held-out founders, and the stated split permits a test skew product to contain one component from a training founder. No analysis establishes that the generated equations correspond to topologically distinct attractors rather than nearby mutations or recombinations of a small number of families.

The external evidence is too narrow for the claims of universal or emergent generalization. Double pendulum is explicitly named as a training founder yet is presented as an unseen real-world system. The PDE study documents only one parameter regime or simulation for each of two PDEs, without independent initial conditions or parameter sweeps; standard errors over correlated windows do not measure model-training or system-instance variability.

Baseline coverage and training budgets are inadequate. The paper omits persistence, linear autoregression, local system-identification, reservoir/NVAR, and relevant PDE forecasting baselines. Chronos-SFT also receives substantially fewer sample exposures than Panda, while Panda additionally receives 200,000 MLM-pretraining iterations, so comparisons are not compute- or data-matched.

The ablations use no independent training seeds, and the claimed MLM benefit is confounded with considerably more optimization and data exposure. No separate validation protocol is described, despite the held-out collection being repeatedly used for architecture selection and analysis.

Central implementation details are missing: parameter-jitter scales, dimensional reconciliation for adding vector fields from systems of potentially different dimensions, chaos-filter thresholds and acceptance statistics, normalization and resampling procedures, optimizer and schedule, and seed selection. No code or dataset availability is provided, substantially limiting reproducibility.

The correlation-dimension calculation is mathematically incorrect. From C(r) proportional to r^D2, the small-distance density scales as r^(D2-1); it is not equivalent to an unbounded Pareto upper-tail fit with D2 approximately equal to alpha. The estimator also ignores its imposed upper truncation, invalidating Figure 17's diagnostic.

The asserted nonlinear resonance is inferred only from qualitative lattice patterns in attention-entropy maps. It measures neither output gain nor a physical resonance response, and lacks an untrained multivariate or architecture-only control; consequently the mechanistic interpretation is unsupported.

Because these issues affect the construction of the benchmark, fairness of the main comparison, and evidence for the real-world and PDE claims, the manuscript is not yet technically substantiated enough for a top-tier acceptance.

There is a fundamental ambiguity in the described architecture. Non-causal self-attention with NoPE is equivariant to permutations of temporal patches, and subsequent mean/max pooling makes the prediction invariant to patch order. The model therefore cannot identify the final patch or use inter-patch chronology as written. Either an essential positional, normalization, or endpoint mechanism is omitted, or the claimed forecasting behavior is technically unexplained.

The baseline comparison is insufficiently controlled. Panda is multivariate and pretrained on the target synthetic domain, whereas most comparators are generic pretrained models and Chronos-SFT is channel-independent. Missing comparisons include matched-capacity multivariate models trained on identical data and compute, classical DMD/reservoir/AR methods, simple persistence or linear baselines, and relevant scientific foundation models.

The external evidence is too narrow and underspecified for claims of universality or emergent PDE forecasting. For the experimental and PDE datasets, the manuscript omits sample counts, preprocessing and normalization, window construction, independence of test windows, spatial resolution, metric aggregation, and detailed uncertainty estimation. A spatially discretized PDE is also itself a finite coupled ODE system, so transfer to two such examples does not alone demonstrate a qualitatively new capability.

The claimed scaling law is based on eight nested dataset subsets without repeated subset draws or training seeds. Consequently, system composition and optimization variance are confounded with diversity; a high fitted R-squared on these points is not sufficient evidence for a general scaling law.

The interpretability claims substantially exceed the evidence. Lattice patterns in attention-rollout entropy under two-tone inputs do not by themselves demonstrate nonlinear resonance, output gain, or a causal forecasting mechanism. Controls using untrained models, phase/amplitude changes, shuffled channels, alternative patch sizes, and models without random nonlinear features are missing; the linear-attention appendix does not characterize the actual softmax model.

The correlation-dimension analysis is mathematically problematic. Small-radius correlation scaling implies a distance density proportional to approximately r^(D2-1), whereas the paper applies an upper-tail Pareto estimator p(r) proportional to r^(-alpha), truncates it between the 5th and 50th percentiles, and then equates alpha with D2. This invalidates the corresponding completion evidence.

Reproducibility is inadequate: there is no code or generated-system release, and important details are absent, including mutation variance, chaos-test thresholds, feature counts and bandwidths, normalization, optimizer and learning-rate schedule, random seeds, baseline configurations, and full data-sampling procedures. The real-data and PDE evidence is too narrow for the broad claims: it covers only three experimental datasets and two single PDE regimes, with unclear sample sizes and undefined standard-error units. The nonlinear-resonance interpretation is unsupported. A lattice in attention-rollout entropy is not a measurement of physical resonance or output gain and could arise from patching, aliasing, or sinusoidal autocorrelation. The appendix's correlation-dimension calculation is mathematically incorrect. From C(r) proportional to r^D2, the small-distance density scales as r^(D2-1), not as a Pareto upper tail r^(-alpha) with D2 approximately alpha. Several headline claims exceed the evidence: the final Panda variant is not defined consistently, masked pretraining can harm rollout, the generated systems' novelty is not demonstrated, and forecasting two discretized PDE trajectories does not establish a universal representation of chaotic dynamics. The claimed scaling law is based on one nested subset at each diversity level and apparently one training run. The architecture is conceptually clean, supports arbitrary channel counts, and incorporates reasonable dynamical inductive biases. The ablations provide useful evidence for channel attention, while the controlled system-diversity experiment is an interesting result.
The manuscript is clearly organized, visually polished, and candid about the mixed effects of masked pretraining and engineered embeddings.
weaknesses: The principal out-of-domain benchmark is generated by the same mutation and skew-product pipeline as the training data. Some test systems may also retain a non-held-out parent component. Without quantitative deduplication, topological-diversity analysis, or evaluation on independently constructed ODE families, this does not fully substantiate the claimed universal generalization.

The baseline comparison is insufficiently matched. Most reported foundation-model baselines are channel-independent, only Chronos is fine-tuned on the proposed corpus, and the paper omits strong multivariate or dynamics-specific alternatives such as a comparably trained multivariate Transformer, VAR/local-linear methods, DMD, reservoir computing, and persistence. Corresponding Panda ablations are not reported on the experimental and PDE benchmarks.

Important reproducibility and evaluation details are absent, including normalization, handling of missing experimental observations, forecast-window counts and sampling, aggregation across channels, optimizer and learning-rate schedule, mutation and random-feature scales, chaos-test thresholds, training-seed variability, and a code or dataset release.

The claimed scaling law is based on one nested subset at each diversity level, apparently without repeated subset draws or training seeds. Consequently, system identity is confounded with system count, and a fitted curve over eight points from one generator is not yet convincing evidence of a general neural scaling law.

The attention analysis does not establish nonlinear resonance. Periodic structure in attention entropy under sinusoidal inputs could arise from dot-product similarity, patching, aliasing, or random initialization; random-weight, shuffled-training, phase/amplitude, and output-spectrum controls are needed.

The correlation-dimension calculation in Appendix E is technically invalid: small-distance Grassberger-Procaccia scaling has density proportional to r^(D2-1), not a Pareto tail r^(-alpha), and the stated Pareto MLE is also inappropriate after upper truncation. This undermines Figure 17.

Several headline claims are stronger than the evidence: the paper evaluates only a small set of experimental and PDE systems, does not evaluate all application domains named in its contribution statement, and the engineered dynamics embedding provides inconsistent benefits in its own ablations. Overall, the ideas and results are promising, but the missing matched baselines and unresolved validity issues place the current version slightly below the acceptance threshold.

weaknesses: The central dataset construction is not specified rigorously enough to reproduce or validate. The defining equation ẋ=κ_a f_a(x)+κ_b ẋ_b is not a complete skew-product definition and is dimensionally ambiguous for parent systems having different dimensions. Mutation scales, selection thresholds, candidate counts, acceptance rates, and several augmentation parameters are omitted.

Calling the procedure an evolutionary discovery algorithm and the resulting 20,000 systems novel is overstated. The described method is essentially parameter perturbation, recombination, and chaos filtering; it has no stated multi-generation process, diversity objective, or quantitative verification that the retained attractors are dynamically or topologically distinct.

The synthetic test set provides weaker evidence of universality than its size suggests. All 9,300 examples derive from a single split of only 20 held-out founder families, many are correlated mutations or recombinations, and a test recombination can apparently contain a parent family seen in training. No repeated leave-family-out splits are reported.

The baseline suite is inadequate for the main claims. Most foundation baselines are channel-independent, only Chronos is adapted to the proposed training data, and there are no strong classical zero-shot baselines such as analog forecasting, locally fitted autoregression, DMD/Koopman methods, or reservoir approaches. A parameter- and training-matched modern multivariate Transformer is also missing. Consequently, improvements cannot be cleanly attributed to the dataset or architecture.

Experimental and PDE evaluations are too underspecified and statistically weak. The paper omits preprocessing and normalization, numbers of independent trajectories or forecast windows, sampling protocols, and the source of several error bars. The three experimental systems have no uncertainty estimates, while the PDE section does not explain spatial resolution, flattening into channels, initial conditions, or train-free model selection. Only two PDEs and weakly turbulent regimes do not support a broad emergent PDE-forecasting claim.

The claimed scaling law is based on one nested sequence of eight datasets and apparently one training run per point. The number of systems is inversely coupled to the number of initial conditions, with no independent subset draws or training seeds. A high R² on these correlated points is insufficient to establish a robust neural scaling law.

The interpretability and nonlinear-resonance claims are largely qualitative. Attention-rollout entropy changes over a very narrow range, and the lattice-like heatmap is not compared against random-weight, phase-surrogate, or suitably matched multivariate controls, nor tied quantitatively to known resonance frequencies or forecasting behavior. Attention textures alone do not establish a mechanism.

With NoPE temporal attention followed by mean or max pooling, the stated network is invariant to permutation of the temporal patches. The paper neither discusses how the forecast endpoint is identified from this unordered set nor provides a patch-shuffling control, leaving an important mismatch between the architecture description and conditional forecasting insufficiently examined.

Appendix E contains a substantive mathematical error. If the correlation integral satisfies C(r) proportional to r^D2, the small-distance density scales as r^(D2−1); the cited Pareto-tail MLE for p(r) proportional to r^(−α) does not yield D2≈α. Fitting distances between the 5th and 50th percentiles also does not establish the r→0 scaling regime. Thus Figure 17 is not a valid correlation-dimension evaluation.

Reproducibility is poor: optimizer, learning rate, random seeds, checkpoint selection, input scaling, exact feature counts, pooling choice, baseline preprocessing, and complete dataset-generation settings are absent, and no code or dataset release is identified. Together with the unsupported universal-representation language, these issues keep the work below the top-tier acceptance threshold.

The architecture and ablations do not convincingly support the claimed innovations. The correlation-dimension analysis in Appendix E is mathematically incorrect. Selecting the 5th-to-50th-percentile distances further does not justify that tail estimator. The completed sequences also retain half of the ground-truth patches, making correlation with the ground-truth estimate partly mechanical.

The attention-entropy lattice is labeled nonlinear resonance without measuring output gain or validating against known resonances. Patch aliasing, sinusoidal periodicity, or architecture-induced structure are plausible alternatives; an untrained-model control, phase/amplitude controls, and quantitative correspondence to a bispectrum or known resonant system are missing. Reproducibility is substantially below the expected standard. The claimed novelty of 20,000 discovered systems is not demonstrated quantitatively: binary chaos filtering of jittered and mechanically recombined known systems does not by itself establish distinct attractors or novel dynamics. Consequently, the results do not distinguish the benefits of the proposed pretraining scheme from the basic advantage of cross-channel access.

The claimed out-of-domain evidence is narrower than presented. Training and synthetic test systems follow the same skew-product generation recipe, and the 9,300 test systems descend from only 20 held-out founders. Descendants and multiple windows are highly clustered, yet the Wilcoxon analyses appear to treat them as independent observations. Cluster-level uncertainty, training-seed variation, and evaluation on independently sourced equation families are missing.

The strong “emergent PDE forecasting” claim rests on only two PDEs and apparently one Kuramoto–Sivashinsky realization and one cylinder-flow simulation. The source of the standard errors and number of independent initial conditions are not reported, and comparisons are again limited to univariate time-series models. Generalization across initial conditions, parameters, spatial resolution, boundary conditions, or PDE families is not demonstrated. The experimental-data studies are similarly underspecified and lack uncertainty estimates.

The central data generator is not reproducible from the manuscript. In particular, adding f_a(x,t) to f_b(y,t) is dimensionally undefined when founders have different dimensions, which range from 3 to 10, unless an unreported projection or pairing restriction is used. Mutation scales, selection thresholds, acceptance rates, generation counts, parent sampling, and several preprocessing choices are omitted; the code and dataset footnotes are blank.

The correlation-dimension estimator in Appendix E is mathematically incorrect. If C(r) scales as r^{D2}, the distance density scales as r^{D2-1}; the Clauset tail estimator for p(r) proportional to r^{-alpha} does not yield D2 approximately equal to alpha. This undermines Figure 15 and potentially the dataset-diversity evidence in Figure 10.

Several evaluation details that could materially affect results are absent. It is unclear whether instance-normalization statistics are computed only from the observed context or from the full trajectory, creating a potential future-information leak. The forecast-window sampling, autoregressive rollout procedure, KL estimator, real-data preprocessing, and PCA fitting protocol are also unspecified. Using sMAPE on zero-centered standardized trajectories is additionally problematic near zero.

Important claims are stronger than the evidence. The generated systems are structured recombinations of a small founder library rather than unconstrained novel dynamics; training samples three coordinates from potentially much higher-dimensional skew systems, making the “trained only on three-dimensional ODEs” characterization misleading. The scaling-law fit uses one run per nested dataset without seed uncertainty or alternative functional fits, while the parameter-scaling study also changes training duration and data. Moreover, Panda's prediction-only Lyapunov statistics are worse than Chronos-SFT despite the long-term-geometry narrative. Overall, substantial work is present, but these soundness, baseline, and reproducibility problems prevent the central conclusions from being competitive at a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and difficult problem: zero-shot forecasting of previously unseen chaotic systems. Its combination of synthetic dynamical-system generation and pretrained forecasting is interesting and potentially impactful.

The central synthetic evaluation is unusually large, covering roughly 9,300 held-out systems, several forecast horizons, multiple pointwise and distributional metrics, and held-out founder lineages rather than merely unseen trajectories from training equations.

The empirical scope is broad, including experimental recordings, two PDE examples, architectural ablations, data-diversity experiments, model scaling, inference-time measurements, and qualitative failure cases.

The architecture is coherently motivated: patching, temporal attention, channel attention, and nonlinear random features are reasonable inductive biases for coupled dynamics. The channel-attention ablations provide evidence that multivariate information is useful.
Panda consistently improves upon the reported time-series foundation-model baselines, and the efficiency advantage over Chronos is practically meaningful.
weaknesses: The baseline suite is not sufficiently diagnostic. Most principal competitors are univariate foundation models and therefore cannot exploit the cross-channel information available to Panda. The paper lacks strong multivariate models trained on the same data and context-adaptive scientific baselines such as VAR, DMD/EDMD, reservoir or next-generation reservoir computing, and persistence. Consequently, the gains cannot be cleanly attributed to the proposed architecture rather than access to coupled channels and task-specific pretraining.

The claimed out-of-domain generalization remains largely within the paper's own generator distribution. The main test systems are produced by the same perturbation, recombination, integration, normalization, and filtering pipeline as training systems, using one split of 20 founder systems. Results over multiple independently sampled founder splits are needed. The real-data experiments and two PDE demonstrations are promising but too small and insufficiently documented to justify broad claims of universal or emergent PDE forecasting.

The dataset-generation method is materially underspecified. Equation (2) adds vector fields from randomly paired systems whose dimensions may differ, without specifying a projection or an equal-dimension pairing rule. Important quantities such as the mutation variance, augmentation parameters, detailed chaos-filter thresholds, number of generations, acceptance rates, and random seeds are absent. Several code/data footnotes are blank, making the central dataset and results difficult to reproduce.

The correlation-dimension evaluation appears mathematically invalid. From the Grassberger-Procaccia relation C(r) proportional to r raised to D2, the small-distance density scales as r raised to D2 minus 1; it is not a decreasing Pareto tail proportional to r raised to negative alpha, and D2 is not approximately the reported Pareto exponent. Thus the completion result in Figure 15, and potentially other correlation-dimension analyses using this estimator, is unsupported.

The claimed scaling law is based on eight nested dataset configurations without reported repetitions across dataset draws or training seeds. The appendix's model-scaling comparison additionally changes parameter count, training iterations, dataset size, initial-condition count, and timescale diversity simultaneously, so it does not isolate parameter scaling.

The long-term-geometry claim is stronger than the evidence. Forecasts extend only to 512 points, the model visibly regresses toward the mean, and the prediction-only Lyapunov-exponent comparisons are worse than Chronos-SFT on several reported measures. Context-plus-prediction metrics are also dominated partly by the shared observed context. Estimation details and uncertainty for KL and spectral metrics are insufficient.

Some interpretability claims are speculative: attention patterns and entropy responses alone do not establish recurrence-map computation, Fourier transforms, or nonlinear physical resonance. These analyses should be presented as qualitative hypotheses rather than mechanistic findings.

strengths: Addresses an important and difficult problem with a coherent combination of synthetic data generation, multivariate pretraining, and zero-shot forecasting.
The 9,300-system synthetic evaluation is extensive, covers multiple horizons and pointwise/distributional metrics, and shows consistent gains over the evaluated time-series foundation models.
Alternating temporal and channel attention is well motivated for coupled dynamics, and the ability to process more channels at inference than during training is useful.
Experiments include architectural ablations, data-diversity scaling, model scaling, inference efficiency, experimental recordings, PDEs, and qualitative failure cases.
The manuscript is generally clear and visually polished, with substantial appendices documenting integration, training, and hardware settings.
weaknesses: The main baselines are predominantly univariate generic forecasters. Comparisons to multivariate PatchTST/iTransformer-style models trained on the same data, reservoir/NVAR/DMD methods, simple persistence or autoregression, and relevant ODE/PDE foundation models are missing. Consequently, the gains do not isolate the value of Panda beyond cross-channel modeling and domain-specific pretraining.

The principal test set is generated by the same mutation/recombination pipeline as training and descends from only 20 held-out founders. Thousands of related descendants are not independent evidence of thousands of distinct out-of-domain families; a single founder split and system-level Wilcoxon tests likely overstate generalization certainty. Repeated family-level splits or blocked bootstrap analyses are needed.

Evidence for the broad real-world and emergent-PDE claims is narrow: three experimental datasets and two PDE simulations at fixed regimes, with unclear numbers of independent trajectories, preprocessing, context selection, and statistical units. The PDE results especially need multiple initial conditions and parameters plus simple and specialist baselines.

The long-term-statistics claim is mixed. The paper acknowledges mean regression, while prediction-only Lyapunov-exponent agreement is poor and worse than Chronos-SFT in Tables 12-13; the stronger context-plus-prediction scores can be dominated by the ground-truth context. KL and spectral estimates are not specified sufficiently to resolve this discrepancy.

The Appendix-E correlation-dimension estimator is technically incorrect as written: from C(r) proportional to r^D, the distance density scales as r^(D-1), not as a Pareto tail r^(-alpha) with D approximately alpha. The fit also ignores upper truncation and temporal-neighbor exclusion. This undermines Figures 10 and 15 and the associated diversity/completion conclusions.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Mutation variance, evolutionary schedule, selection thresholds, rejection statistics, seeds, and several evaluation details are absent; Equation 2 does not define how unequal-dimensional parent vector fields are coupled; and the supplied manuscript has blank code/data footnotes. It is also unclear whether instance normalization uses context-only statistics, which is necessary to exclude future-information leakage.

Ablation and scaling conclusions lack training-seed uncertainty. The largest-model comparison changes model size, iterations, dataset size, initial-condition count, and timescale distribution simultaneously, while the proposed dynamics embedding is not consistently beneficial.

The claimed novelty of 20,000 discovered systems is somewhat overstated: they are structured skew-product compositions and parameter perturbations of 129 curated systems, and the paper does not establish how much genuinely new dynamical behavior this construction adds beyond the parent library.

strengths: The paper tackles an important problem: zero-shot forecasting of unseen chaotic systems rather than fitting a separate model to every system.

The main synthetic benchmark is unusually large and covers multiple horizons and pointwise, spectral, and distributional metrics. Panda consistently outperforms several time-series foundation models, including Chronos fine-tuned on the same corpus, while offering much faster inference.

Channel attention is well motivated for coupled dynamics, and the same-data ablations provide useful evidence for it. Tests on experimental data and two PDEs are promising demonstrations of broader transfer.
The manuscript is generally clear, visually polished, and commendably candid about mean regression and the adverse effect of masked pretraining on rollout performance.
weaknesses: The claimed out-of-domain generalization is weaker than presented. All 9,347 principal test systems come from the same mutation, coupling, integration, and filtering pipeline as training and descend from only 20 held-out founders. A single lineage split does not establish robustness to genuinely different equation families, and lineage dependence is not accounted for in uncertainty estimates or significance tests.

The baseline suite does not adequately isolate the source of the gains. There is no strong multivariate forecaster trained from scratch on the same corpus, nor classical dynamics baselines such as autoregression, DMD/SINDy, reservoir computing, or context-fitted local models. Comparisons are dominated by pretrained univariate models with substantially different tokenization and objectives.

The experimental and PDE evaluations are insufficiently specified and appear narrow. Sample counts, window construction, preprocessing, missing-value handling, and statistical uncertainty are largely absent. The PDE evidence covers only two systems at one configuration each, apparently using a single trajectory, while the vortex experiment uses a PCA basis derived from the simulated data. This is not enough to support a broad claim of emergent PDE forecasting.

The proposed scaling law is based on one nested sequence of eight datasets and apparently one training run per point. It lacks seed-to-seed uncertainty and independently sampled system subsets, and simultaneously trades system diversity against the number of initial conditions. The result convincingly indicates a diversity trend, but not yet a robust neural scaling law.

The appendix's correlation-dimension estimator is technically incorrect. From the Grassberger-Procaccia relation C(r) proportional to r^D, the small-distance density scales as r^(D-1). The paper instead fits an unbounded Pareto tail p(r) proportional to r^(-alpha) over the 5th-50th percentiles and equates alpha with D, while also ignoring upper truncation. Consequently, the reported correlation dimensions and the associated completion/diversity conclusions are not validated.

Evidence for preservation of long-term geometry is mixed: Panda visibly regresses toward the mean, and its prediction-only Lyapunov-exponent R-squared and correlation are worse than Chronos-SFT. The KL estimator is not described sufficiently to assess finite-sample bias when comparing short predictions with 4,096-point trajectories.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The displayed code and dataset footnotes are empty, while essential details such as mutation scales, selection thresholds, number of evolutionary generations, treatment of unequal-dimensional parents in the additive coupling, normalization statistics, and several real-data evaluation protocols are missing. Overall, the work is promising and close to competitive, but these technical and evaluation gaps place it slightly below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and ambitious problem: zero-shot forecasting of unseen nonlinear dynamical systems. The evolutionary construction of roughly 20,000 chaotic ODEs is creative and potentially valuable beyond this particular model.

Panda combines patching with temporal and channel attention in a sensible dynamics-aware architecture. The ablations provide concrete evidence that cross-channel modeling is important, especially for coupled systems.

The synthetic evaluation is unusually large, covering approximately 9,300 held-out systems, multiple forecast horizons, several pointwise and distributional metrics, statistical tests, qualitative examples, and documented failure modes.

The results against general time-series foundation models are consistently favorable. The experiments on experimental recordings and two PDEs are particularly interesting evidence of cross-domain transfer from synthetic ODE training.

The fixed-data scaling experiment provides an insightful result: diversity across governing systems appears more valuable for out-of-system generalization than additional initial conditions from fewer systems. weaknesses: The principal baselines are univariate general-purpose time-series models. The paper lacks competitive multivariate models trained on the same data and classical dynamics baselines such as vector autoregression, reservoir/next-generation reservoir computing, or Koopman-style predictors. Consequently, it is difficult to separate the benefits of multivariate modeling and synthetic supervision from Panda-specific innovations.

The 9,300 test systems are correlated descendants of only 20 held-out founders and use the same recombination, filtering, timescale normalization, and augmentation pipeline as training. It is unclear whether test recombinations may contain one non-held-out parent. Results on the held-out founder systems themselves are only qualitative, so the effective breadth of the synthetic generalization evidence is smaller than the nominal test-set size suggests.

The experimental and PDE evidence is promising but limited to three real datasets and two simulated PDE settings. Sample counts, window construction, preprocessing, and uncertainty are insufficiently documented, and no strong multivariate or PDE-oriented baseline is included. Thus, the claim of an emergent general PDE-forecasting capability is stronger than the current evidence.

The correlation-dimension derivation appears mathematically incorrect as written. For C(r) proportional to r^D, the small-distance density scales as r^(D-1); fitting a lower-bounded Pareto tail p(r) proportional to r^(-alpha) and identifying D with alpha is not equivalent to the Grassberger-Procaccia estimator. This undermines Figure 15 and potentially the related dataset-diversity analysis.

The scaling studies are confounded: model size changes together with training iterations, dataset size, number of initial conditions, and period distribution, while the scaled Chronos-SFT baseline receives substantially less training throughput. The diversity scaling law also appears based on one nested dataset/model run per scale rather than independent training replicates.

Reproducibility remains incomplete. The code/data links are blank, key mutation and attractor-filter thresholds are omitted, Eq. 2 is under-specified for parents with different state dimensions, and it is unclear whether test-time normalization uses context-only statistics. If C(r) scales as r to the power D2, the distance density scales as r to the power D2 minus 1; fitting an unbounded tail model p(r) proportional to r to the power minus alpha over the 5th-to-50th-percentile range and setting D2 approximately equal to alpha is not equivalent. The claimed scaling law is fitted to only eight nested dataset configurations without repeated subset draws or training seeds. Model size, training duration, dataset version, initial-condition count, and temporal-period diversity are additionally changed together in the scaled-up experiments.

The skew-product equation adds vector fields from founder systems whose dimensions range from three to ten, without explaining how unequal dimensions are reconciled. The mutation variance, attractor-test thresholds, candidate counts, acceptance rates, and purported evolutionary generations are also missing. Code and checkpoint links in the reproducibility statement are blank.

The normalization protocol is ambiguous: the manuscript says entire trajectories receive instance normalization but does not state whether statistics are computed only from each forecast context. Computing them using future targets would leak test information.

The correlation-dimension estimator in Appendix E appears mathematically incorrect. For small distances, the Grassberger-Procaccia relation implies a distance density proportional to r^(D2-1), not a Pareto tail r^(-alpha); moreover, the stated Pareto MLE is applied after upper truncation. Equating its alpha with D2 therefore lacks justification, weakening the dataset-diversity and masked-completion results based on this quantity.

Long-horizon conclusions depend strongly on the metric. Panda looks favorable under the authors' custom GMM KL estimator, but the alternative geometric-misalignment implementation ranks Chronos-SFT ahead at every reported horizon, while DynaMix and Chronos-SFT outperform Panda at long horizons. On the final 2,048 forecast steps, Panda is the worst reported model because of mean regression. The abstract and main discussion overgeneralize the distribution-preservation evidence.

The 9,347 test systems are correlated descendants of one randomly chosen set of only 20 held-out founders. There are no repeated founder splits or training seeds, so the effective sample size is unclear and the extremely small per-system p-values may overstate robustness. Likewise, the proposed scaling law is based on one nested dataset and apparently one training run per point, without uncertainty across runs or comparison of alternative functional fits.

The real-data evaluations lack basic protocol details such as the number and placement of windows, preprocessing, uncertainty, and statistical tests. The attention-entropy patterns are also labeled nonlinear resonance without a mechanistic definition, causal intervention, or adequate null models, making the interpretability claim speculative.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: transferable forecasting of unseen chaotic systems rather than fitting a separate model to each system.
Constructing a large synthetic corpus from many chaotic ODE families is promising, and withholding founder systems and their descendants is conceptually stronger than a random trajectory split.

Panda combines patching with channel attention in a sensible permutation-compatible architecture. The reported short-horizon improvements over generic time-series foundation models are substantial in MAE, cover several horizons, and are supported by useful component ablations.

The evaluation is unusually broad, spanning thousands of synthetic systems, three experimental datasets, two PDEs, long rollouts, computational efficiency, and several pointwise and distributional metrics.
The appendix commendably discloses unfavorable results, including mean regression at long horizons and an alternative KL estimator under which Panda loses to baselines.
weaknesses: The dataset-generation method is not reproducible as written. The mutation scale, selection thresholds, candidate/acceptance statistics, and several other procedural choices are missing, while the code and checkpoint links in the reproducibility statement are blank. More fundamentally, the additive coupling in Eq. 2 is dimensionally undefined when the two parent vector fields have different dimensions, although founders reportedly range from 3D to 10D; no projection or matching rule is specified.

The evidence for genuinely out-of-distribution generalization is weaker than presented. All 9,300 synthetic test systems descend from only 20 held-out founders and are consequently highly dependent; there is only one founder split, and it is unclear whether test systems can have a training-seen co-parent. Significance tests appear not to account for lineage-level dependence, making the extremely small p-values uninformative. Multiple independent family splits with lineage-level aggregation are needed.

Baseline parity is inadequate for the main architectural claim. Most competitive foundation-model baselines are univariate and therefore cannot exploit coupling; DynaMix is evaluated under a setting the authors repeatedly acknowledge is mismatched. Missing comparisons include comparably trained multivariate transformers, an architecture-matched PatchTST/channel-mixing baseline, and strong classical dynamics methods such as DMD, autoregression, or reservoir computing.

The PDE claim is not convincingly established. It covers only two systems, while the FNO and DeepONet baselines use one-step training and are explicitly labeled non-comparable. The comparison therefore cannot support broad claims of emergent PDE forecasting or superiority to trained operator-learning approaches.

The long-term distributional conclusion is metric-dependent and overstated. Panda's advantage under the custom GMM KL estimator disappears or reverses at longer horizons. Under the alternative geometric-misalignment estimator, Panda is 11.9% to 32.9% worse than the best baseline, and on the tail-only evaluation its KL divergence is 15.25 versus 3.50 to 9.68 for the baselines. This conflicts with the abstract's broad claim of preserving distributional measures.

The correlation-dimension analysis contains a mathematical error. From the Grassberger-Procaccia relation C(r) proportional to r^D, the small-distance density scales as r^(D-1); fitting a Pareto tail p(r) proportional to r^(-alpha) and setting D approximately equal to alpha is not equivalent. This undermines the completion result, its interpolation comparison, and part of the dataset-diversity validation.

The experimental-data evaluation is too under-specified to verify: preprocessing and resampling, handling of missing values, numbers of windows or trials, uncertainty, and numerical aggregate results are absent. It largely consists of one qualitative figure and comparison only against Chronos-SFT.

Normalization and timescale handling need clarification. The manuscript says entire trajectories are instance-normalized and rescaled using dominant-period information, but does not state that test normalization statistics are computed from context only. Using forecast-region statistics would leak future information, while global period standardization substantially simplifies the claimed zero-shot problem.

The claimed scaling laws are not isolated convincingly. The diversity experiment uses one sequence of nested subsets without independent training seeds, while parameter-scaling experiments simultaneously change model size, optimization steps, dataset size, numbers of initial conditions, and period distributions.

The attention interpretation is speculative: patterned entropy maps are labeled nonlinear resonance without measuring physical gain or establishing a causal connection to forecasting, and visual attention structures alone do not demonstrate the asserted computation. Overall, these soundness, evaluation, and reproducibility problems outweigh the paper's promising premise and positive short-horizon results.

All 9,347 test systems come from only 20 held-out founders and the same skew-product generator, integration pipeline, timescale normalization, and selection rules used for training. Results are based on one founder split and apparently one training seed; family-level aggregation, multiple held-out splits, and seed uncertainty are needed.

Grassberger–Procaccia estimates the small-radius slope of log C(r) against log r; the manuscript instead fits a Pareto tail p(r) proportional to r^{-alpha} over the 5th–50th percentiles and identifies alpha with D2. The asserted equivalence is false, undermining the completion result in Figure 18/Table 10 and any dataset-diversity conclusions using this estimator.

Long-horizon preservation is not robust to the metric. The alternative geometric-misalignment KL estimator favors Chronos-SFT over Panda at every reported horizon, and on the final 2,048 rollout steps Panda is dramatically worse than Chronos-SFT and DynaMix. The claimed scaling laws are confounded. The data-diversity curve uses eight nested subsets without repeated subset draws or training seeds, so subset composition can explain the fit. The model-size study simultaneously changes training iterations, dataset size, number of initial conditions, and timescale distribution, preventing attribution to parameter scaling.

The interpretability claim is unsupported: structure in attention-rollout entropy is labeled “nonlinear resonance” without measuring output gain, relating patterns to known resonances, using untrained/positional controls, or performing causal interventions. The real-data evidence is narrow and underdocumented: sample counts, window selection, preprocessing, uncertainty, and significance are largely absent, and comparisons are mainly against Chronos. It is also unclear whether instance-normalization statistics are computed from context only; using full trajectories would leak future information.
